amendments.why: Rule 17's waw-relative sentence withholds the relative from the waw wherever an explicit subject pronoun stands in the clause, but the reason the rule itself gives for that condition is that a present pronoun takes the relative before the waw does. JDG.17.2 is the case the sentence did not consider: אַתְּ stands in the clause but the ASV writes thou for it and the relative points at the silver, so the pronoun is not what the relative realizes. Read literally, the over-broad condition left the verse pass heading a which on a pronoun meaning thou while the word writing that lexeme sat in the verb's unit, against rule 24 — which is exactly the error this reconciliation patched. The amendment narrows the condition to a pronoun the relative realizes, states the count, and disposes of a preposition the ASV supplies before such a relative. Nothing in the corpus contradicts it: a waw aligns to which in ten units and to who in twenty-four, and the explicit-pronoun cases the rule cites (וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו, וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי) are untouched, since in both the pronoun is the relative's own referent and no separate pronoun is written.
amendments.rule: An inflected verb may align to an English subject pronoun, auxiliary, and main verb together. Choose the lexical English verb as the target head. **This permission is specific to a pronoun realizing the verb's person and number.** A lexical English subject noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal is present answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit: `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* gives *shall dwell* to the verb and leaves *men* `added`. **A volitive English frame belongs to the verb whose mood it renders.** Where the ASV expands an imperative or jussive with *Oh* or *Oh that ... would*, the framing words join the verb's unit and the unit heads on its lexical predicate: `הוֹדוּ` → *Oh give thanks* heads on *thanks* under rule 44, and `יוֹדוּ` → *Oh that ... would praise* heads on *praise*. A lexical subject noun supplied inside that frame is still `added` under the preceding sentence — *Oh that men would praise* leaves *men* outside the verb's discontinuous unit. This applies only where no optative particle or multi-source optative idiom stands in the Hebrew; a present `לוּ` or `מִי יִתֵּן` takes its own fixed English formula under rule 30. **A presentative dummy *there* is not such a lexical subject.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb or participle with a presentative frame — `יֵּצֵא` → *there came forth*, `נִשֵּׂאת` → *there was lifted up* — the dummy belongs to the verb's unit, by the same constructional reasoning that puts it on `הָיָה` under rule 21, and the unit still heads on the lexical verb. When the verse also has an explicit subject noun, that noun's tokens are its own unit and only a genuinely pleonastic pronoun stays with the verb. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus an explicit subject pronoun as a relative clause, the English *who* or *which* realizes the pronoun; the waw is `unrepresented` if the ASV writes no separate connective.** Do not give the relative pronoun to the waw merely because it opens the recast clause: `וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו` → *which was behind him* gives *which* to `הוּא` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and `וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי` → *who am old* gives *who* to `אֲנִי` on the same terms. **But read whether the relative is what realizes that pronoun before applying that sentence.** What it governs is a recasting in which the pronoun itself becomes the relative, which is why the ASV writes no other word for it and the relative's referent is the pronoun's own. Where instead the ASV writes the pronoun's own English word beside the relative, and the relative points at something else the clause speaks of, the pronoun is holding a rendering of its own and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, while a relative pointing at another antecedent realizes nothing of it and would head on a word that does not write its lexeme, against rule 24: the pronoun takes the word written for it, the finite verb keeps its auxiliaries and lexical verb, and the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective, exactly as it is where no pronoun stands at all. `וְאַתְּ אָלִית` → *about* ***which*** ***thou*** *didst utter a curse* gives *thou* to `אַתְּ`, *which* to the waw and *didst utter a curse* to the verb, while the supplied *about*, whose relation no morpheme carries, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, since no bare nominal stands for rule 33 to place it on. Read whom the relative refers to and count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; one verse may write both shapes, and JDG.17.2 does, aligning `אֲנִי לָקַחְתִּי` → *I took* with the pronoun holding its own *I*. **A question auxiliary the ASV fronts belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb.** English marks a yes-or-no question by fronting an auxiliary, and where `הֲ` stands in the clause that word is what the ASV has written for it: `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause that has no verb at all to take it, and `הַעַל אֵלֶּה לֹא אֶפְקֹד` → *Shall I not visit* gives *Shall* to `הֲ` and *I visit* to the verb, even though that auxiliary also carries the imperfect's future. The `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question is read the same way, since it is what marks that clause as the second question: `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* gives *will* to `אִם` and *ye tremble* to the verb. **But a particle for which the ASV has written a connective of its own is not a home for the auxiliary as well.** Where the ASV renders that `אִם`, or another particle standing at the head of the second question, by a written *Or*, *Or if* or another connective, that word is the particle's under rule 14, the particle takes no second English word, and the fronted auxiliary is the ordinary one this rule's first sentence gives the verb: `אִם יְדַבֵּר אֵלֶיךָ רַכּוֹת` → ***Or*** *will he speak soft words unto thee* gives *Or* to `אִם` and *will he speak* to the verb. This is the reasoning of this rule's second limit below, where an interrogative holding an English word of its own leaves the auxiliary to the verb, and of rule 51's ruling that a waw holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second word. Count the clause's English function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; where the ASV writes no connective for the particle, the preceding sentence governs as before. Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: `הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ` → *Fear ye not me*. Two limits. Where no interrogative morpheme is present at all, a fronted *do* is the verb's own under this rule's first sentence: `לֹא שָׁפָטוּ` → *do they not judge*. And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole. **And a particle heading an indirect question takes the subordinating word the ASV writes for it, which puts it in that same position.** Where `הֲ` introduces a question embedded under a verb of testing, seeing, knowing or asking and the ASV writes *whether* or *if* at the head of the embedded clause, that word is what the particle is rendered by: the particle takes it and heads on it, and a modal or auxiliary the ASV fronts inside that clause belongs to the predicate under this rule's first sentence. `לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת בָּם אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל הֲשֹׁמְרִים הֵם אֶת־דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה` → *that I may prove Israel,* ***whether*** *they* ***will keep*** *the way of Jehovah* gives *whether* to `הֲ` and *will keep* to the participial predicate, while the explicit pronoun keeps only its own *they* under rule 20. This is the count the paragraph above runs, read for the first question rather than the second: a particle already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and giving it both would leave the predicate's auxiliary unaccounted against rule 2. The corpus aligns an interrogative `הַ` to *whether* in six units. Read what the ASV has written before reaching for this sentence: where it marks the embedded question by the fronted auxiliary alone and writes no subordinator, the particle takes that auxiliary as in a direct question, and where it writes neither, the particle is `unrepresented` as above. **An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun in that clause is realized by that relative, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a pronoun the relative realizes takes it before the waw does, but a pronoun standing in the clause under an English word of its own is not such a pronoun, and without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.

conventions: Relative recastings in this chapter: the relative goes to the morpheme it actually realizes, and to the clause's waw only when no morpheme does. A pronominal suffix takes whose (17.1); an explicit subject pronoun whose referent is the antecedent takes who (17.7); the waw takes who where nothing in the clause points at the antecedent (17.4, 17.5) and takes which in 17.2, where אַתְּ holds the thou written for it and the relative points at the silver. A waw whose relative another morpheme has taken is unrepresented (17.1, 17.7).

היה or a verbless clause with dative לְ + suffix and a לְכֹהֵן predicate occurs three times, and the suffix takes the possessive the ASV writes on priest each time: his in 17.5 and 17.12, my in 17.13, where the same suffix is also realized as the I of I have and both words are its one discontinuous unit headed on I (rule 18). The dative לְ is unrepresented throughout (rules 40, 43); the resultative לְ on כֹהֵן is unrepresented where the ASV writes no preposition (17.5, 17.10 twice, 17.12) and takes the written to in 17.13 (rule 49).

אֶלֶף וּמֵאָה -> eleven hundred is one noncompositional unit of אֶלֶף and מֵאָה with the intervening waw unrepresented (17.2, 17.3): the English compound is a rendering no morpheme owns a part of, no and stands between the numerals (rule 42), and the source head goes to מֵאָה, whose lexeme hundred writes, rather than to the first-token fallback (rule 6).

מִלֵּא אֶת־יַד -> consecrated: the verb and יָד share one unit headed on the verb, and the object marker is unrepresented (17.5, 17.12). The ASV margin's literal gloss filled the hand of corroborates the fusion and decides nothing (rules 7, 38).

The italic pieces the ASV supplies after a numeral of silver names the unit the money is counted in, not the numeral's own lexeme, so it is added under rule 33's supplied-measure-noun clause rather than joining the numeral under rule 31 (17.2, 17.3, 17.4, 17.10). The same reading gives the italic a place its own added unit after find (17.8, 17.9).
בֵּית לֶחֶם arrives as two Np tokens and each takes the English word written for it (Beth, lehem) rather than fusing; the following יְהוּדָה takes the qualifying judah (17.7, 17.8, 17.9).

This is the count the paragraph above runs, read for the first question rather than the second: a particle already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and giving it both would leave the predicate's auxiliary unaccounted against rule 2. The corpus aligns an interrogative `הַ` to *whether* in six units. Read what the ASV has written before reaching for this sentence: where it marks the embedded question by the fronted auxiliary alone and writes no subordinator, the particle takes that auxiliary as in a direct question, and where it writes neither, the particle is `unrepresented` as above. **An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun in that clause is realized by that relative, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a pronoun the relative realizes takes it before the waw does, but a pronoun standing in the clause under an English word of its own is not such a pronoun, and without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.
amended.why: Rule 17's waw-relative sentence withholds the relative from the waw wherever an explicit subject pronoun stands in the clause, but the reason the rule itself gives for that condition is that a present pronoun takes the relative before the waw does. JDG.17.2 is the case the sentence did not consider: אַתְּ stands in the clause but the ASV writes thou for it and the relative points at the silver, so the pronoun is not what the relative realizes. Read literally, the over-broad condition left the verse pass heading a which on a pronoun meaning thou while the word writing that lexeme sat in the verb's unit, against rule 24 — which is exactly the error this reconciliation patched. The amendment narrows the condition to a pronoun the relative realizes, states the count, and disposes of a preposition the ASV supplies before such a relative. Nothing in the corpus contradicts it: a waw aligns to which in ten units and to who in twenty-four, and the explicit-pronoun cases the rule cites (וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו, וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי) are untouched, since in both the pronoun is the relative's own referent and no separate pronoun is written.

report: Two real splits, both in the recastings. The rest of the candidate table is the ASV rendering one word differently in contexts the source licenses: מן as out of before a place name in 17.7-8 and of in 17.9, כסף as silver/money, לְ before an infinitive as to (17.3, 17.8, 17.9, 17.11) and as the subordinator as (17.8), הלך as departed and went, היה as was/became/have, and בית as a construct with a supplied the beside the toponym element of Beth lehem.

Split 1, JDG.17.13. The chapter writes היה or a verbless clause plus dative לְ plus suffix plus לְכֹהֵן three times. In 17.5 and 17.12 the suffix takes the possessive the ASV writes on priest (his), the dative לְ going unrepresented under rule 40. In 17.13 the same suffix took only the I of I have, and the answering my was marked added under rule 18's closing sentence — but that sentence is conditioned on no suffix being present, and one is (the י of לִי). Rule 18's twice-realized-suffix sentence governs instead: I ... my is that suffix's one discontinuous unit, headed on I, the direct pronoun rather than the possessive recasting, exactly as מִכֶּם מָזוֹר -> cure you of your wound heads on you. Patched; the verse loses that added unit.

Split 2, JDG.17.2. Four clauses in this chapter are recast as English relatives: 17.1 gives whose to a suffix, 17.7 gives who to an explicit הוּא whose referent is the antecedent and leaves the waw unrepresented, and 17.4 and 17.5 give who to the waw where no morpheme points at the antecedent. 17.2 gave the which of about which thou didst utter a curse to אַתְּ while the answering thou went to the verb as its subject pronoun, so the one morpheme meaning thou held a relative whose referent is the silver while the word that writes its lexeme sat in another unit, against rule 24. The same verse aligns אֲנִי לָקַחְתִּי the other way (I on the pronoun, bare took on the verb), so nothing in the source licenses the difference.

The 17.2 patch: אַתְּ takes thou, the verb keeps didst utter a curse headed on curse, the waw takes the which under rule 17's waw-relative sentence (the corpus aligns a waw to which in ten units and to who in twenty-four), and the supplied about, whose relation no morpheme carries, is its own added unit. The competing reading — about which added whole under rule 55, the waw unrepresented — is named in the unit note under rule 8.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The five waws are recast-relative waws (17.1, 17.2 as repatched, 17.7) and the numeral-phrase waws of eleven hundred (17.2, 17.3), unrepresented under rules 17 and 42; the אֶת of 17.3 and the nine לְ are the documented rule 16, 21 and 40 conventions; the suffixes at 17.5 and 17.8 and the articles at 17.6 and 17.13 are words the ASV does not write; and the ה of שְׁבָה at 17.10 is tagged Sh, not Sd, so rule 32's first sentence and not its directive-he clause governs. BSB attaches all of these to their host words by its own convention.

Also checked and left alone: נַעַר -> young man headed on young in 17.7, 17.11 and 17.12 (rule 31's tie-breaker does not reach it, since מַן is not נַעַר's lexeme the way man is אֱנוֹשׁ's), the italic pieces added in four verses and a place added in two, the fused מִלֵּא אֶת־יַד -> consecrated in 17.5 and 17.12, and בַּאֲשֶׁר -> where in 17.8 and 17.9. All are internally consistent.

Six conventions recorded, one amendment to rule 17 proposed: its waw-relative sentence excluded any clause where an explicit subject pronoun stands, when what should exclude the waw is a pronoun the relative actually realizes. That over-broad condition is what produced the 17.2 error.
